name: SLAC-MIT deep inelastic electron scattering
notes: Start date conflict: Taylor writes that the first inelastic experiments "began in August 1967"; Kendall writes "In late 1967 the first of a long series of experiments ... was started". Chosen: August 1967 (the more specific statement).

End date: Riordan gives the series as 1967-1973; the Nobel press release says the work was carried out at the end of the 1960s and beginning of the 1970s; Kendall says measurements continued well into the 1970s. Chosen: 1973, approximate.
The collaboration record is created because the bar asks for one where a collaboration exists (the brief did not list it); the integrator may drop it. No detector records (not assigned).

physics_goals.quote: The essence of the SLAC-MIT experiments was to observe how a beam of electrons at high velocities (energy from 4 GeV to 21 GeV) is affected when it is led through a target consisting either of liquid hydrogen or of deuterium.
physics_goals.value: Observe how a beam of electrons is affected when it passes through liquid hydrogen or deuterium targets, measuring the scattered electrons

summary.plain: From 1967 MIT and SLAC physicists fired electrons from the new SLAC linear accelerator at hydrogen and deuterium targets. Hard knocks off the proton came out as if from tiny hard grains inside it, the first clear sign of the quarks.
summary.technical: Inelastic e-p and e-d scattering, 4-21 GeV beams, 8 GeV and 20 GeV magnetic spectrometers in End Station A; first inelastic runs from August 1967; scaling of the structure function νW₂ with ω = 2Mν/q² reported at Vienna in August 1968 and in Phys. Rev. Lett. 23, 935 (1969).

unique_capabilities.quote: Unlike in earlier investigations, electron beams of record-high energies were now available. These beams were supplied by a two-mile-long linear accelerator at SLAC, which afforded a “microscope” of higher resolution than earlier.
unique_capabilities.value: Electron beams of record-high energy from the two-mile linear accelerator
